comments.text:
China seems to be ain a much better position than hinted here. It's industrial sector is now far superior than what the US and Europe currently have, even including Canada. It has a near monopoly on critical minerals. It is the one best equipped to transition away from fossil fuels. It's military production outpaces that of all its adversaries. It's debt can be much more manageable with a productive and growing economy backed by more than just software. One issue is that its economy depends on exports. Currently, that is what slows down its growth the most. But it can be fixable. It's biggest issue is population decline. That may bring down its superpower status in a few decades, but the other powers have more pressing problems.

The US will quickly lose the ability to defend its interests abroad. The gutting of its stockpile, the collapse of confidence in both its commitments and its ability to deliver, and the purging of its top military leaders at the Pentagon have seriously fragiled the superpower. While it maintains a military industrial base, it is so skewed towards fighting insurgencies from the 2000s and early 2010s that it looks completely incapable of producing at levels required to sustain a major conflict against a peer adversary. Finally, the US also completely depends on its currency remaining the reserve currency to fund itself. But the significant drop in confidence in its administration and institutions has shaken that foundation. When allies such as Canada and the European Union are actively working on reducing the dependency on the USD to do international trade, that foundation is starting to look shaky as hell.

Europe has the advantage of remaining stable, and with reduced US influence, can look forward to increasing private investments flowing in. Its main disadvantage is the near deadlock of the EU agenda, blocked by individual countries applying vetoes, failing to ratify agreements, etc... That, and the uncertainty of France's future, are slowing it down. Honestly, as Europe rearms itself, it's going to be a toss-up for second place between the US and Europe.

The idea that "correlation implies causation" is an example of a questionable-cause logical fallacy, in which two events occurring together are taken to have established a cause-and-effect relationship.
